section_1.title: Introduction: The Chaos of the Coffee Cup
section_1.content: Define turbulence as a multi-scale energy cascade. Briefly introduce the Reynolds Number (Re = ρvL/μ) as the ratio of inertial to viscous forces, determining when flow transitions from laminar to turbulent.
section_1.example: Visualizing a drop of milk hitting coffee: it starts as a smooth plume (laminar) before breaking into intricate, unpredictable swirls (turbulence).

section_2.title: The Kolmogorov Hypothesis (1941) & The 5/3 Law
section_2.content: Introduce the concept of 'Local Isotropy' and the energy cascade. Present the Kolmogorov-Obukhov spectrum, E(k) = Cε^(2/3)k^(-5/3), where E(k) is energy density, k is wavenumber, and ε is dissipation rate.
section_2.example: An animation showing a large vortex (the 'parent') breaking down into smaller vortices (the 'children'), representing energy transferring from low-k (large scales) to high-k (small scales).

section_3.title: Universal Constants and Scaling
section_3.content: Discuss the Kolmogorov constant (C ≈ 1.5). Explain that despite the complexity of the Navier-Stokes equations, the statistical structure of turbulence is universal in the 'inertial range'.
section_3.example: Comparing a massive ocean current eddy and a small puff of smoke; despite size differences, their mathematical spectral signature (the -5/3 slope) remains identical.

section_4.title: Visualizing the Mathematics: The Energy Spectrum Plot
section_4.content: Display a log-log plot of Energy vs. Wavenumber. Label the 'Inertial Range' where the -5/3 slope dominates, distinguishing it from the 'Energy Containing Range' and 'Dissipation Range'.
section_4.example: A 'Digital Bird' character flying through a flow field; as it hits different zones, the screen displays a real-time 'heat map' of the energy spectrum, showing the slope steepening as the bird reaches the viscous dissipation region.

section_5.title: Synthesis and Summary
section_5.content: Recap how mathematical constants transform chaotic fluid motion into predictable statistical models. Reiterate that turbulence is not just randomness, but a governed process of energy degradation.
section_5.example: Final summary slide: An astronaut (or drone) navigating through turbulent air, using the 5/3 law to predict and compensate for incoming gusts.
